extracted.intended_audience: Patent and trademark practitioners (registered attorneys and agents), law firms, and others who practice before the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and disciplinary standards governing conduct before the USPTO (OED): statutory/regulatory authority, timing and sources of grievances, common causes of disciplinary complaints, applicable rules (37 C.F.R. Part 11), and illustrative disciplinary decisions and consequences. Useful for practitioners to understand obligations and avoid sanctionable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority for OED regulation of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) authorizes the Office to establish regulations that may govern the conduct of agents, attorneys, or other persons representing applicants or other parties before the Office; 35 U.S.C. § 32 authorizes the Director to suspend or exclude from further practice any person shown to be incompetent, disreputable, guilty of gross misconduct, or who does not comply with regulations established under §2(b)(2)(D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the legal foundation for OED discipline. See also Bender v. Dudas, 490 F.3d 1361 (Fed. Cir. 2007). Compliance with Office regulations (37 C.F.R. Part 11) is mandatory; violations can lead to suspension or exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for disciplinary actions (statute of limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA amended 35 U.S.C. § 32 to require disciplinary proceedings to be commenced not later than the earlier of: (1) 10 years after the misconduct occurred, or (2) one year from when the misconduct was made known to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 34(a) explains that proceedings begin with the filing of a complaint; § 34(d) specifies timing for filing a complaint shall be within one year after the date on which the OED Director receives a grievance. 37 C.F.R. § 11.1 defines 'grievance' as a written submission presenting possible grounds for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources and initiation of grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: An investigation may be initiated pursuant to information from any source suggesting possible grounds for discipline. (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(a)). Common sources include clients, colleagues, USPTO exam corps (patent/trademark), published decisions, news articles, and other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a duty to report professional misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 11.803). Grievances are written submissions received by the OED Director presenting possible grounds for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent causes of grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: Common categories that generate disciplinary complaints: Neglect; Dishonesty, Fraud, Deceit, Misrepresentation; Fee-Related Issues; Unauthorized Practice of Law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These high-level categories frame complaints OED receives and guide both prevention and investigation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect (failure to handle matters competently and timely)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: failure to reply to Office actions; failure to communicate with client; failure to reply to client inquiries; failure to report Office communications; failure or delay in filing patent applications; failure to revive or assist in reviving abandoned applications; failure to turn over files to new representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples (In re Gibson; In re Frantz; In re Tachner) show consequences ranging from public reprimand to exclusion or multi-year suspension. Practitioners are responsible for adequate internal organization, systems, staffing, and equipment to manage client matters and avoid neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct includes concealing information from client (e.g., date of Office action, date/reason for abandonment), misrepresenting status of an application, making false or misleading statements to USPTO (examiners, TTAB, PTAB), to revive applications, to obtain extensions, or in response to OED inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include fabricating filings or USPTO receipts, creating phony correspondence, billing for unperformed services, and misappropriation of funds. Case outcomes include public reprimand, suspension, and exclusion (In re Goldstein; In re Chan; In re Hicks; In re Reardon). Such conduct is among the most serious bases for exclusion from practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee-related misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Improper fee-related practices include repeated failure to reply to fee-related Missing Parts; failure to return client's advanced fees; improper commingling of client funds with practitioner funds; checks returned/EFTs dishonored for insufficient funds; failure to disclose fee escrow or business relationships with invention development companies; charging excessive interest on unbilled fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples (In re Scott; In re York; In re Riley; In re Peterson; In re Lane) show a spectrum of sanctions from public reprimand and probation to suspension or exclusion depending on severity (e.g., theft from client account leads to exclusion). Maintain formal accounting records and avoid commingling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized Practice of Law (UPL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice before the Office includes law-related services connected with presentation to the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)). Unauthorized practice examples: non-attorneys practicing in TM matters; patent agents practicing in TM matters or state law; unregistered individuals practicing patent matters; excluded or suspended practitioners continuing practice; foreign attorneys practicing without authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (In re Walters; In re Seto; In re Zborovsky; In re Rayve; In re Jaeger; In re Campbell) show sanctions for practicing outside one's authorized scope or jurisdiction, failing to notify OED of employment changes, and practicing while suspended. Practitioners must make clear the scope of their authorization and withdraw when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct outside direct case-handling that negatively affects fitness to practice, such as abusive or expletive-laden communications to judges and improper communications with tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Tassan — leaving expletive, abusive voicemails to TTAB judges led to reprimand, prohibition on communications with TTAB judges for two years, and an anger management requirement. Non-technical misconduct can carry disciplinary consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of disclosure vs. client confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: When a practitioner learns information material to patentability in a client matter, the duty of disclosure to the Office can be an exception to client confidentiality rules. Mandatory exception: 37 C.F.R. § 11.106(c); permissive exceptions may exist in state ethics rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must balance ethical confidentiality with disclosure obligations under patent law; if the client won't consent to disclosure, consider ethical and patent/court contexts and applicable rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts arise when current representation conflicts with prior or concurrent representations (example: a firm hired to defend Widget Corp. while having previously performed prosecution for Research Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicts can impede representation and may require withdrawal or other remedies. Practitioners must identify and manage conflicts consistent with 37 C.F.R. Part 11 and applicable state rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safekeeping client property and forwarding materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must safeguard client property and promptly forward client materials (example: forwarding the 'ribbon copy' of an issued patent to the client).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to forward property or withholding client materials can reflect poorly on fitness and lead to discipline. Maintain systems to deliver client property upon issuance or termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminating representation and withdrawal obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a practitioner must withdraw (e.g., due to conflict, change of employment, or client termination), they must comply with rules on withdrawal, correspondence address changes, and preserving client interests. Practical problems include inability to change correspondence address without power of attorney and obligations when client delays in taking action (e.g., pre-payment of issue fee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 C.F.R. § 11.116, MPEP 402.06, and USPTO form PTO/AIA/83 for resources. Practitioners should ensure proper filing of powers of attorney, effecting correspondence address changes, timely notice to clients, and facilitating transitions to new counsel to avoid abandonment or prejudice to client rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. Part 11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopted effective May 3, 2013 (78 Fed. Reg. 20179), 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101-11.901 (with prior Part 10 rules applying before that date). The rules are based on the 2011 ABA Model Rules, and include sections on Client–Practitioner Relationship, Counselor, Advocate, Transactions with Persons Other Than Clients, Law Firms and Associations, Information About Legal Services, Maintaining the Integrity of the Profession, and a savings clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must follow Part 11 provisions (e.g., §§ 11.101–11.118; §§ 11.201–11.204; §§ 11.301–11.309; §§ 11.401–11.404; §§ 11.501–11.507; §§ 11.701–11.705; §§ 11.801–11.804; § 11.901). Comments/annotations to the ABA Model Rules are non-binding but informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'practice before the Office' (scope of regulated activities)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b): 'Practice before the Office' includes, but is not limited to, law-related service that comprehends any matter connected with the presentation to the Office relating to a client's rights, privileges, duties, or responsibilities under the laws or regulations administered by the Office for the grant of a patent or registration of a trademark, or for enrollment or disciplinary matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities constituting practice include rendering opinions on patentability and trademark registration, and representing clients in OED matters. Those performing such activities must be properly authorized/registered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to report professional misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a duty to report professional misconduct as set forth in 37 C.F.R. § 11.803.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners who learn of another practitioner's misconduct may have an obligation to report; this is also a source of grievances and initiates OED investigation if submitted as a 'grievance'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and types of discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: OED may impose public reprimand, probation, suspension for a specified number of years, or exclusion from practice before the USPTO depending on the severity of the misconduct (as reflected in case examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples show mounting sanctions for repeated or serious misconduct: public reprimand (lesser offenses), probation, multi-year suspension, and exclusion (e.g., misappropriation or fabrication leading to exclusion). Remedies and sanctions are applied based on facts, severity, harm to clients, and patterns of behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resources for reviewing discipline decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions imposing public discipline are available in the FOIA Reading Room and in the Official Gazette for Patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retrieve discipline cases via http://e-foia.uspto.gov/Foia/OEDReadingRoom.jsp (select 'Decision Type' = 'Discipline' and click 'Get Info'). Use published discipline decisions to study precedents and understand OED's enforcement patterns.
